mode: Built-in ImageGen, edits of a Godot reference. Concept images, no runtime assets.
heroOfPlate: The same V3 central hoard is registered in both variants using the native camera. Front corridor and terrain are retained outside the room-wall band.

outputs.prompt: Use case: precise-object-edit. Edit this actual Dungeon Empire mobile game capture as an art-direction mockup. Keep the original 960:600 composition exactly aligned: same camera at 2:1 isometric angle, same scale, footprint, square room of 2x2 logical cells and ONE completely open, walkable entrance towards the lower-left corridor. NO DOOR, no gate, no entrance arch. Retain the existing dark navy indigo chunky beveled masonry, size of stones and black grout lines, minimal flat painterly shading and simple shapes. The ordinary corridor at lower-left stays absolutely untouched and should contrast with the purpose-built treasury room. Important: change only the four room wall segments and corner caps within the existing perimeter, NOT the floor or its slate tiles, NOT the cave exterior, NOT the corridor, zoom, angle or entire room. The front wall stays short to see inside, matching shield-height of the surrounding masonry. Far room walls can rise by one course (maximum about 35 pixels in reference) to accommodate the special bays. No tall pillars, roofs, freestanding furniture, people, torches, chests, piles on the floor or centerpieces. Keep the middle empty so a single treasure hoard can be placed by the game. The art is deliberately robust and a little menacing, for a dungeon master's treasury; the special construction must read in a thumbnail, but it is still the same dungeon. Architectural details belong IN the wall and terminate precisely at the room/corridor junction: broad strokes, no miniature filigree, cinematic light, photorealism, captions, or HUD. Keep blue masonry overwhelmingly dominant and metal accents old/dark. Return one clean view. DIRECTION A, THE TREASURER'S COUNTING HOUSE. Build broad deep recessed, rectangular counting niches IN the two far walls, one bay per grid step, four bays total. Give these bays actual thick stepped slate lintels and small squat dividers with a continuous heavy stone sill mortared into the adjacent stone. It is furniture carved into masonry, NOT chests, freestanding shelves, window openings or doors. Dark closed niche backs make the recess evident. Two of the four niches hold a short stack of tiny gold coins on a ledge on one side; others have a plain bronze weighing pan or a stone tally tablet in relief, readable but secondary to the architecture. Add a single carved round coin seal on the back corner cap and one coin-stamped cap on the short front corner, replacing the existing diamond cap. Make the course of the low front walls slightly more dressed with a narrow bevel echoing the rear sill. Maintain the left corridor walls in their original plain blue two courses terminating at the chamber threshold. This is a dark counting room integrated into the original tile kit.

Unlike a series of display niches, both far walls should be deliberately SOLID. Rebuild their mid-level masonry as TWO broad bas-relief panels made from large indigo ashlar with visible grout lines. On each is a single carved round seal of the master's coin with a small raised angular lozenge on it, a legible old-bronze rim and deep recessed blue centre. A heavy ribbed stone pilaster binds the back corner, simple chamfered coping continues around the perimeter and steps down neatly at the threshold. Cut a continuous horizontal narrow frieze INTO the stone courses that links the two coin reliefs and follows the isometric wall line, then terminates cleanly at the corridor. The low front walls repeat the carved coping but leave the room plainly visible. Optional ONE muted violet inset in the rear pilaster, no additional violet lighting or crystals; maximum TWO round reliefs, NO repeating gold plaques on every brick. Bold simple stone depth, grooves and broken outlines; never ornate Versailles palace, aureate railings, bank cages, gate, vault door, or coat of arms. The room's treasury identity comes from the minted coin reliefs and stonework itself.
